rationale: Deuteronomy 24:14-15 says, "Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy," and "You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them" (BSB). In the parable, "When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, 'Call the workers and pay them their wages'" (Matthew 20:8, BSB). In Greek, Matthew's ἀπόδος αὐτοῖς τὸν μισθόν and the Septuagint's αὐθημερὸν ἀποδώσεις τὸν μισθὸν αὐτοῦ (Swete) share the verb and its object, though "give back the wage" is also ordinary Greek for paying anyone. Four commentators on 20:8 name the law. Ellicott: "It was one of the humane rules of the Mosaic law that the day-labourer was to be paid by the day, and not made to wait for his wages (Deuteronomy 24:15). This law the householder keeps, and his doing so is a feature in his character." The Pulpit Commentary: "According to Mosaic Law (Deuteronomy 24:15), a hired labourer was to be paid his wages at sunset." Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites the verse for "the reckoning time between masters and laborers," and Gill cites it through Maimonides. Leviticus 19:13 gives the same rule ("You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand," BSB). Matthew names no source, and the shared wording is common wage language; what the commentators trace is a legal background the story keeps rather than a text it cites. So the type is allusion and the label plausible, as with conn-matt18-rebuke-lev19 and conn-matt16-leaven-exodus12.
